item.title: Behavioral Fine-Tuning Without the Tuning
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: A 90 MB language model that talks in something resembling my voice, served from this static blog with no backend. There was no training run. No weights moved. Instead: a token-level n-gram over my own corpus, mixed into the LLM's output distribution at sample time. The fine-tune is a corpus plus an index plus a sampling loop.
item.content:encoded:
There is a 90 MB language model on this site that answers questions in something resembling my voice. It was not fine-tuned. The model’s weights have not been touched.

What is happening, instead, is that at every generation step the model’s output distribution is being mixed in probability space with a token-level n-gram trained on every word I have published on this blog. The mix is a literal linear combination. The “fine-tune” is a corpus, an index over that corpus, and a sampling loop.

You can try it at /ask, with a slider for how strongly the prior pulls. The same machinery, with a much bigger corpus, is at /alex.

This post is about how it works, why it works, and what this kind of architecture lets you do that gradient-descent fine-tuning cannot.

The Setup

Three pieces:

  1. A small language model in your browser. SmolLM2-135M, 360M, or 1.7B Instruct, served from HuggingFace as quantized GGUF, run via Wllama’s WebAssembly port of llama.cpp. Pure CPU, no GPU. The 135M variant is about 90 MB on disk; the 1.7B is a gigabyte. All three share the same SmolLM2 BPE tokenizer.

  2. A token-level n-gram over my blog corpus. Every post on this site, tokenized with that same SmolLM2 BPE, indexed with a suffix array. About 1.6 MB of source text, 470,000 tokens, a 1.9 MB suffix array. The browser fetches both binaries once, holds them as Uint32Array views, runs O(m log n) lookups for any continuation query.

  3. A token-by-token generation loop that mixes the two distributions.

That third piece is the trick.

The Math

At each generation step the LLM produces a probability distribution p_llm(t) over its 49,152-token vocabulary, exposed by Wllama’s getLogits(-1) after the softmax. The infinigram, given the longest suffix of the current context that occurs in the corpus, produces a sparse distribution p_ngram(t): nonzero on tokens that the corpus has actually seen following that context, zero elsewhere.

The mixture is a literal linear combination:

p_mix(t) = α · p_ngram(t) + (1 − α) · p_llm(t)

Sample from p_mix, append the chosen token to the context, repeat.

That is the whole algorithm. In actual JavaScript, the inner loop is small enough to fit on screen:

for (let step = 0; step < N; step++) {
  const llm = await wllama.getLogits(-1);          // [{token, p}, ...]
  const m = ig.longestSuffixMatch(context);        // longest in-corpus suffix
  const ngram = m.suffixLen > 0
    ? new Map(ig.continuations(m.matchedTokens).map(c => [c.token, c.prob]))
    : null;

  const mix = new Map();
  for (const { token, p } of llm) {
    const pn = ngram?.get(token) ?? 0;
    mix.set(token, alpha * pn + (1 - alpha) * p);
  }

  const next = sample(mix, temperature);
  if (await wllama.isTokenEOG(next)) break;
  context.push(next);
  await wllama.decode([next]);
}

No log-space arithmetic, no smoothing tricks, no logit-bias hacks. Tokens unseen by the n-gram have p_ngram(t) = 0, so they retain (1 − α) · p_llm(t) in the mixture. They are not zeroed out; they just lose the additive lift that corpus-supported tokens get.

When α = 0 you get the LLM. When α = 1 you get the n-gram, which loops as soon as the generated context drifts off-corpus. Between those endpoints, the LLM provides grammatical structure and the n-gram provides register.

Why It Works

Two surprises, in order.

The first is that tiny language models are mostly capacity for grammar. Most of the parameters in a 135M model are spent learning to compose words into syntactically plausible sequences. Knowing what the writer should say next is a separate skill, and it is the skill that does not fit. A small model has all the basic English machinery and almost no register, almost no preferences, almost no taste.

The second surprise is that an n-gram is enough to supply that taste, if the n-gram is built over your own text. An n-gram is famously a weak language model on its own, because it does not generalize. But I do not want it to generalize. I want it to provide a contextualized empirical distribution over what I would have written next, given what has just been written. That is a register prior. The n-gram is exact, byte-perfect, traceable to actual occurrences. Every word it lifts in probability is a word I actually wrote.

The mix exploits the asymmetry. The LLM is good at grammar and bad at register. The n-gram is bad at grammar and good at register. Compose them in probability space and you get a hybrid where each component does the thing it is good at.

What “Fine-Tuning” Means Here

Conventional fine-tuning takes a pretrained model and runs gradient descent on a smaller, more specific dataset. The weights move. Afterward, the model produces text that pattern-matches the training distribution. The fine-tuned weights are an approximate, compressed, lossy representation of that distribution, learned by trial.

What we are doing here is structurally different. The corpus stays uncompressed. The LLM weights do not move. At sample time, two distributions are produced and mixed.

A few implications of that structural difference:

  • Adding a document to your fine-tune is a corpus rebuild, not a training run. Add the text, re-tokenize, rebuild the suffix array (~30 ms in C). Done.
  • Removing a document is the same operation in reverse. There is no question of whether the model “forgot” it. The corpus does not contain it any more, so the n-gram cannot lift its probabilities. There is no leakage from a forgotten gradient.
  • Inspecting the fine-tune is reading the corpus. There is no opaque weight blob. The “voice prior fine-tuned on Alex’s blog” is literally Alex’s blog plus an index.
  • Auditing a generated phrase for memorization is one binary search. If the model produced a long verbatim run, it is because the corpus contains exactly that run, and you can locate every occurrence.

You cannot easily do any of those things with gradient-descent fine-tuning. You have to prompt-probe a black box and hope.

Tokenizer Parity Is Load-Bearing

For the mix to be coherent, both distributions must be over the same alphabet. The LLM emits logits over its 49,152 BPE tokens. The infinigram has to produce probabilities over those same tokens, indexed the same way.

The corpus is tokenized once, offline, with HuggingFace’s AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct"). The browser does the same, via Wllama’s GGUF-embedded tokenizer, on user input and during streaming output. Both produce identical token IDs because they are the same BPE, byte for byte.

This is what makes the architecture clean. Three model sizes (135M, 360M, 1.7B) all share the SmolLM2 BPE, so the same suffix array works against any of them. Swapping models in the UI is a URL change. If I wanted to try Qwen 2.5 or Llama 3.2 instead, I would need to retokenize the corpus with that model’s tokenizer and rebuild the SA, which would take a few minutes in Python. The browser code would not change.

Two Pages

/ask is the version trained on edited blog prose: 1.6 MB of formal writing, 213 posts, polished register. The model picks up paragraph rhythm, common phrasings, project names. Output sounds like an essay.

/alex is the version trained on my entire text orbit: blog posts, every question I have ever typed into ChatGPT, every assistant response I have read. About 60 MB of source text, 16 million SmolLM2 tokens, 60 MB suffix array. Three registers stitched together in conversation order: essay, conversational question, ChatGPT-verbose.

The longest-suffix matching does the routing. When the generation context looks like the start of an essay paragraph, the longest match falls in the blog portion of the corpus and the prior pulls toward essay register. When it looks like a chat reply, matches come from the assistant turns. When it looks like a question, from the user turns. The corpus is heterogeneous; the prior is contextually appropriate at every step, because the suffix array always finds the closest precedent regardless of register.

The /alex page is an experiment in how far you can push a personal corpus into a model. The signal is denser than blog-only, but ChatGPT’s verbose register dominates the byte count, so at high α the model drifts toward chatbot voice. At low α (0.05–0.15), the prior just nudges word choice while the LLM stays in charge of structure.

Why It Has To Run Locally

The whole pipeline runs in the browser because that is the only way the architecture stays honest. No backend, no API key, no telemetry. The corpus is the same one I publish. The LLM weights are public. The mixing happens in user space. Anyone who wants to see what is being applied to the model can read the code on the page.

This is also the use case that fine-tuning has historically been worst at: people who want to make a personal model out of their own writing but do not want to run a GPU cluster, do not want to upload their writing to anyone, and do not want a single-shot opaque-weights artifact they cannot inspect. Mixing-at-sample-time with a token-level n-gram is what fine-tuning probably should have looked like for that use case all along. The model is a public utility; the personalization is a 2 MB artifact you build yourself in fifteen minutes and ship as a static asset alongside your blog posts.

What This Architecture Cannot Do

It does not give the model new abilities. The LLM still knows what the LLM knows. The n-gram cannot teach it new skills, only nudge its outputs toward the register of an existing skill. If the LLM cannot multiply three-digit numbers, no amount of register prior will fix that.

It does not generalize beyond the corpus. The n-gram is exact-match. It cannot pull in concepts I have written about in a paraphrased way; it can only lift words I have actually used. If the LLM proposes a token I have never typed, the prior has no opinion.

It does not work well at high α with a small corpus. The n-gram needs enough data to produce a varied next-token distribution. With 1.6 MB of source text and α near 1, the model loops as soon as the generated context drifts off-corpus.

It does not produce model weights. There is no artifact you can ship to a different runtime. The “fine-tune” is a corpus plus an index plus a sampling loop. That is also the point.

What’s Next

The infinigram mixing is one half of a larger story. The other half is paragraph-level retrieval, mixed with the same kind of probability-space combination. Right now the n-gram operates at token granularity; a passage-level version would let the model paraphrase ideas from my corpus without quoting verbatim. That requires a different lookup data structure (probably an embedding index instead of a suffix array) and a different mixing strategy, but the principle is the same: the corpus stays uncompressed, every retrieval traces to source, the model is steered at inference time without modifying weights.

For now the toy works. It is a 90 MB language model that talks like me, served from a static blog with no backend, with the corpus and index as static assets a curious reader can download and inspect. That feels like the right shape for personal AI. Small, local, inspectable, and fine-tuned on your own text by definition.

Try it: /ask, /alex, and the infinigram explorer.
